pictureNote: draws this register as a diagram, laid out on the server. It adds the three things a table of relationships has nowhere to put: how many applications are configured to use each partner, how many people have signed in through each application and relationship pair, and what the identity-provider side is configured to do about authenticating somebody — including where one relationship brokers to another, which is what makes this service an identity bridge and is invisible in any single row.
noneMatches: No federation relationship matches. The filter above may be hiding some.
noneConfigured: No federation relationship is configured. Nothing federated happens until one is — and then not until it is enabled, which is a second, deliberate act.
oneDirection: One relationship is one DIRECTION. A partner this service both consumes from and asserts to is two relationships with two ids, because everything that configures one differs by direction — the endpoints are theirs or ours, the certificate is theirs or ours, the attribute mapping runs inbound or the release list runs outbound.
stillToSetRefuses: {missing} still to set. It refuses rather than half-working.
createdDisabled: It is created disabled, whatever is filled in here, and nothing about it does anything until it is enabled on its own page. That is not caution for its own sake: a partner that half-exists and silently accepts assertions is the failure this whole register is arranged to prevent, and enabling is the second, deliberate act that says the configuration is finished.
idRules: The id is the key, the RDN and a URL segment, so it has to start with a letter or a digit and hold only letters, digits, dot, dash and underscore. Partner is their own identifier in whatever their protocol calls it, and on a service-provider-side relationship it is CHECKED: an assertion whose issuer is not that string is refused, even when the signature verifies.
caveatRefusal: This is the one feature here that has to be configured before it will do anything, and the one page in this console that configures a REFUSAL. Everywhere else this service accepts what it is given — any username, any client_id, any entityID, any LDAP bind. It cannot do that at an assertion consumer service: what arrives there is an unauthenticated HTTP request claiming to be a person, and the session it would produce is the same one /oauth2/authorize, /wsfed, /saml2 and this console all read. A permissive version of it would not be a permissive mock; it would be an authentication bypass for every protocol in this process.
caveatSigner: The gate is on the SIGNER, and on the SUBJECT too (#109). A verified assertion signs in only the person its partner's subject is LINKED to — a federationLink on the entry. What happens to a subject nobody linked is the relationship's fedSubjectPolicy: the person it names signs in here first and is then linked (link-at-first-sign-in, the default), it is refused (pre-linked), it gets a new entry of its own (jit-namespaced), or — in development only — the old name match (any-existing). Three rules narrow it further, and a console administrator is refused unless fedMayAssertAdministrators is on. Nothing is written onto an entry before all of that has passed.
linkDirectoryView: the register as the directory sees it
notFoundA: There is no federation relationship called
notFoundB: . Unlike almost everything else in this console, one does not appear because somebody used it: this register is configured and nothing creates an entry in it by turning up.
neverPrinted: Never printed on this page or in the audit log, though an ldapsearch of this directory will show it — see the note at the foot.
linkedSignsIn: Each person below carries a federationLink through this relationship: the partner's identifier for them, which is what signs them in. Under fedSubjectPolicy {policy}. A link is added and removed on the person's own page, and removing one ends the sessions this partner signed them in to.
linkedSignalsOnly: Each person below carries a federationLink through this relationship, written by an administrator on the person's own page: the issuer and subject the partner's iss_sub events name them by, or opaque and the opaque id. It signs nobody in; it is how this partner's events find the person (#374).
nobodyLinked: Nobody is linked to this partner yet.
noneRelease: None — and that means no release policy rather than release nothing. This partner receives exactly what /admin/claims and /admin/saml-attributes would give anybody. Adding the first name here starts filtering..
enabledNotConfiguredWarn: Enabled and not configured. {missing} still to set. Every endpoint for this relationship refuses in this state rather than half-working — a federated sign-in that got half way and produced a session would be the worst possible outcome.
noApplicationNamed: none named — this relationship configures nothing until one is
headingConfigureAtPartner: What to configure at the partner
configureAtPartnerNote: These are the URLs to give whoever runs the identity provider. The assertion consumer service is the one that matters: a partner sending its answer anywhere else produces a 404 in a browser AFTER a successful sign-in somewhere else, which is the least diagnosable failure this feature has.
entityIdSameString: the same string, deliberately: one name for this service per partner, so a partner keying its trust store off an entityID gets one that is only ours-with-them
metadataUnsigned: unsigned, deliberately — a signature over it made by the very key it publishes proves nothing they did not already have to trust
signOutSingleLogout: SingleLogoutService (Redirect and POST), for the partner's LogoutRequest and its LogoutResponse to ours
signOutCleanup: Sign-out cleanup URL, for wsignoutcleanup1.0 — the person confirms it here
signOutPostLogout: post_logout_redirect_uri, for a sign-out here that ends at the partner
noSignOut: none — {protocol} defines no sign-out, so the partner cannot end a session here and is not told of one ending
noCertificate: none — rotate the key below to issue one
startSignIn: Start a federated sign-in through this partner
willRefuse: — it will refuse until this relationship is enabled and configured
whatItDoesNote: Every protocol endpoint here already issues to anybody that asks, so this relationship changes nothing about whether the partner is answered. What it adds is two things: the partner is marked as a FEDERATION PARTNER rather than a test client, and fedRelease below decides which attributes are released to it.
releaseOnlyA: The release list can only remove, and only from what
releaseOnlyB: and the groups claim would add.
releaseOnlyC: It cannot touch sub, iss, exp, a NameID or anything else the protocol puts in an artifact itself — those are what make the artifact verifiable, and a release list that could drop iss would produce tokens that fail to verify with nothing pointing back at this page.
deleteNote: The entry goes and takes its {count} recorded sign-in(s) with it. The PEOPLE it authenticated keep their entries under ou=users — nothing is ever deleted from there — and any session they hold is unaffected until it expires or is ended.
oneEntryNote: Everything on this page is an attribute on one directory entry, so an ldapmodify of {dn} does exactly what these forms do — two doors onto one register, not two registers. That cuts both ways: fedClientSecret is this service's own credential AT the partner, held in the clear, in a directory where every bind succeeds. It is never shown here and never written to the audit log, and anybody who can read this directory can authenticate as this service at that partner. A deployment federating with something real should know that. The Shared Signals credentials, fedSignalsClientSecret and fedSignalsBearer, are sealed under the key-encryption key wherever keys persist (#373).
everyArrivalA: Every arrival from every partner is on
signalsSignsIn: The partner's CAEP and RISC events about the people it signs in. A verified one is acted on as the signal-response policy permits — by default ending the sessions THIS relationship started for the person, and on account-disabled blocking its sign-ins of them until its account-enabled. A local sign-in and every other partner are untouched.
signalsOnly: This partner signs nobody in: it only sends CAEP and RISC events. By default they are recorded and nothing more, except a device's compliance, which is set. Its people are the ones linked to it below (<iss> <sub>, or opaque <id>), or matched by mail where fedSignalEmailMatch is on.
givenWithStream: given to the partner with the stream
noEventsListed: None: the stream asks for whatever the partner supports.
plaintextRefused: A plaintext assertion is refused. The partner must encrypt to the key above, with the algorithms above.
allowUnencryptedA: fedAllowUnencrypted is on: a plaintext assertion is ACCEPTED
allowUnencryptedB: , and the person's identifier and attributes may cross their browser in clear.
plaintextDevelopment: A plaintext assertion is accepted in development mode; product mode refuses it. An encrypted one is decrypted and held to the algorithms above in both.
rotateNote: A new key is issued under this realm's Intermediate and published at once; the one it replaces still decrypts for {seconds} seconds (federation.encryptionKeyGraceS).
headingSignalsSent: Shared Signals this service sends the partner
signalsSentNote: The streams on this service's own transmitter that the partner's application {application} owns. Read only: a stream belongs to the receiver that created it, and is managed through SSF's stream management API.
noOutboundStream: The partner's application holds no stream here.
unmappedNote: Names this partner sent at a sign-in that were NOT written to the directory: nothing maps them, or a mapping sends them onto an attribute no partner may write. The newest first; a name is kept for as long as minted state is (persistence.mintedRetention).
mapOneRealm: This is one trust realm. The federation register is per realm — an id that names a relationship in another realm names nothing here — so this picture is of {realm} and of nothing else. The realm switcher at the top of the page is how you get to another one, and the realm is drawn on the hexagon so that a saved copy of this document still says which realm it is of.
mapLeftRight: Left asks, right authenticates. Everything on the left of the hexagon arrives wanting somebody signed in — an application here, or a foreign service provider. Everything on the right is a party this service asks to do the signing in. An identity-provider-side relationship therefore points INWARD even though this service asserts outward, because the arrow is the request; and an identity BROKER, which is both at once, is then a single straight line through the middle instead of two arrows leaving the same box.
mapEmptyHeadline: This realm federates with nobody, so there is nothing to draw.
mapEmptyB: and does nothing until it is enabled, which is a second deliberate act. Federation is the one feature in this service that must be configured before it will do anything at all.
mapRowsB: shows, plus the two columns that are facts about TWO registers rather than about one entry: how many applications are configured to use a partner, and what the identity-provider side does about authenticating somebody. Neither has anywhere to live on a relationship's own entry.
perRelationshipNote: One row per application and relationship, which is the pair the counts on this page are of. fedAuthentications on a relationship answers "how much has crossed this partner"; this answers "how much has crossed it for each of the applications behind it", which is a different question the moment a second application names the same partner. A pair is counted only where this service is CONFIGURED for it — the application entry names the relationship, or an identity-provider-side relationship brokers to it — and the check is made against the live register when the sign-in completes rather than trusted from the request that started it.
keptRatherThanDropped: These sign-ins happened and are kept rather than dropped, so the relationship's own totals still add up. Something named this pair when they happened and no longer does.
noApplicationConfigured: No application is configured to authenticate through any relationship in this realm, and none has ever done so. That is appFederationRelationship on an entry under ou=applications, which is written by nobody — no protocol presents it and no sighting derives it.
unattributedNote: Some sign-ins belong to no row above, and that is not a fault. A relationship's own total counts every credential that crossed it; the rows above count only the ones that named an application this service is configured for. Three ordinary things make the difference: the partner buttons at the foot of the sign-in screen belong to no application, {path} needs no configuration at all to reach, and a sign-in naming an application that does not point here is refused a row and logged. The difference is named rather than left to be noticed — this is a page about counting, and a column that does not add up is worse than one that explains itself.
keyNote: The shapes and the colours are drawn by the same render() the picture is, so a legend cannot come to describe a diagram this service no longer draws.
drawingNoPan: . It does not pan or zoom: it is generated on the server and arrives as markup, which is what keeps this console free of scripts. The SVG document does zoom.
oneApplicationTitle: An identity-provider-side relationship names exactly one application, in fedApplication. There is no count to make.
nothingCountsTitle: Nothing counts sign-ins on this side. What fedAuthentications counts is assertions CONSUMED, and an identity-provider-side relationship issues them — so the figure would be zero however busy the partner was.
brokerNotUsable: that relationship is not usable, so the sign-in screen is drawn instead
notAMechanism: not a mechanism this service has
authAtPartnerTitle: The authentication happens at the PARTNER on a service-provider-side relationship, so there is nothing here to configure.
